Navel wounds

One calf study reported earlier stump separation, faster healing, and fewer cases of omphalitis and mortality with added phototherapy.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

One calf study reported earlier stump separation, faster healing, and fewer cases of omphalitis and mortality with added phototherapy.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact veterinary category contains one publication and one calf study, rather than multiple independent cohorts. The study compared phototherapy plus iodine with iodine alone in 57 neonatal dairy calves. It reported faster stump separation and healing in the light group, but this result has not been independently replicated in the category. (de Souza Faria et al. 2017)

Human and clinical evidence

No human clinical evidence applies to this veterinary indication. The study was conducted in newborn calves and should not be interpreted as evidence for human umbilical wound care.

Animal evidence

The controlled study included 57 calves, with 28 receiving phototherapy plus topical iodine and 29 receiving iodine alone. The authors reported earlier umbilical-stump detachment, faster navel healing, and lower omphalitis and mortality in the treated group. Allocation and outcome assessment limitations, alongside the single-study evidence base, mean that the observed differences require replication.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No cell, tissue, or ex-vivo study is listed in the exact neonatal navel-wound category. The evidence is a veterinary clinical study.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The reported treatment used a 640 nm visible red LED, 300 mW output, and 46.8 J/cm² for 60 seconds at four points, once daily for three days. Iodine was also used in both groups. These settings describe one protocol and should not be assumed to be interchangeable with laser treatment or other wound-care settings.

Interpretation

One controlled study in newborn calves reported earlier stump separation, faster healing, and fewer cases of omphalitis and mortality with added phototherapy. This single veterinary result needs replication under routine farm conditions and does not establish an effect in people.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for calf navel healing. One controlled study reported faster healing and earlier umbilical stump separation.
Publications and records1 unique title in Veterinary medicine > Bovine: navel wounds.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Evidence comes from one controlled veterinary study of 57 newborn calves. The reported outcomes favor added light treatment, but replication is absent and iodine was part of both care pathways. Further work should use concealed allocation, blinded wound scoring, adequate follow-up, and prespecified infection and survival outcomes.
